questions.q: What is the relationship between an endpoint and a deployment in this SDK workflow?
options: They are the same thing, just different names
An endpoint is the container; a deployment is the model running inside it
A deployment is created first, then wrapped in an endpoint
An endpoint can only ever hold exactly one deployment
questions.explain: A ManagedOnlineEndpoint is created first as a container, then one or more ManagedOnlineDeployment objects are deployed into it.

questions.q: What percentage of traffic does a brand-new deployment receive by default?
options: 0% — it must be explicitly routed to
100%, automatically
50%, split with the previous deployment
Traffic routing is not configurable
questions.explain: A fresh deployment starts at 0% traffic even after it finishes provisioning — the endpoint.traffic assignment explicitly routes requests to it.

questions.q: Which two fields confirm a deployment is actually live and serving requests?
options: CPU usage and memory usage
Model name and model version only
Provisioning state and Deployment state
Instance count and VM size
questions.explain: Provisioning state (Succeeded) confirms the resource was created, and Deployment state (Healthy) confirms the model is actually serving requests.

questions.q: In the Python SDK code shown, what does InteractiveBrowserCredential do?
options: It silently fails if no credential is cached
It stores a password in plaintext in the script
It disables authentication entirely
It opens a browser sign-in window the first time it's used
questions.explain: InteractiveBrowserCredential pops open a browser window for sign-in the first time the code runs, which is expected behavior.

questions.q: What proves the deployment deliverable is actually done, according to this lesson?
options: A real response comes back from invoking the endpoint, not an error
The endpoint name sounds correct
The portal shows the model card
The deployment YAML file was saved locally
questions.explain: Sending a real request and getting a real response back — not an error or timeout — is the concrete proof this deliverable is complete.
